stem.en: Two ice skaters stand still, facing each other. Skater A (40 kg) pushes off Skater B (80 kg). By Newton's third law, the push each one feels is equal in size. Using F = ma as well, who ends up moving faster?

text.en: Skater A, the lighter one — the same force acts on both, but A's smaller mass means a = F ÷ m works out to a larger acceleration (and speed) for A.

feedback.en: Correct — this is the canoe-and-battleship idea again, just with two people instead of a boat: equal forces, unequal masses, unequal outcomes.

text.en: Skater B, the heavier one — more mass means more push-back force overall.

feedback.en: The third law already fixes the two forces as equal, regardless of mass — mass doesn't change the SIZE of the force pair. What mass changes is each skater's acceleration for that shared force.

text.en: Both move at exactly the same speed — Newton's third law says the effect on each is always identical.

feedback.en: This is exactly the mix-up the canoe-and-battleship example warned about: 'equal forces' does not mean 'equal effects.' The third law fixes the force; F = ma decides that a smaller mass gets a bigger acceleration from that same force.

explanation.en: Same setup as the canoe and the battleship, different costumes: the third law hands both skaters the identical-sized push, but F = ma means that identical push produces a bigger acceleration on the smaller mass. Skater A (40 kg) ends up moving faster than Skater B (80 kg) — in fact, exactly twice as fast, since acceleration (and here, resulting speed) is inversely proportional to mass for equal forces.

hints.en: The forces on both skaters are equal — that's the third law. What differs between the two skaters that could still make their outcomes different?
a = F ÷ m. Same F for both — which mass gives the bigger a?
